what: The Unix Timestamp Converter translates between epoch time, the number of seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, and ordinary dates. It shows the current timestamp live and converts in both directions, in any time zone.

Developers, system administrators, data analysts and testers use it to read timestamps in logs, databases, APIs and JWT tokens, to create timestamps for tests, and to check what time an event happened in another part of the world.
It understands seconds, milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds, handles daylight saving time, and runs in your browser.
uses: Paste timestamps from server logs to see when something happened in your own time.
Check created_at and expires values stored as epoch numbers.
Turn a date and time into a timestamp for a test, script or database query.
See the same moment in UTC, your zone and any other zone.
Paste a column of timestamps and get ISO dates for all of them.
tutorial: The top boxes show the current Unix time in seconds and milliseconds, updating live. Press Copy to copy either one.
Paste a number into Unix timestamp. The unit is detected from the number of digits; change Unit if needed. Commas and spaces are ignored.
You get the date in your time zone and in UTC, ISO 8601, RFC 2822, a relative time like "3 days ago", and the value in seconds and milliseconds. Each line has a Copy button.
Choose a zone under Also show in time zone to add that local time and its ISO 8601 form with the offset.
Convert a date to a timestamp
Under Date to timestamp, pick a date and time and the time zone that date is in. The timestamp in seconds and milliseconds appears below.
Paste one timestamp per line into Convert many at once and press Convert list. Each line gets its ISO date in UTC and your local time.
features: Current Unix time in seconds and milliseconds.
Uses your browser's full time zone list with daylight saving rules.
Local, UTC, ISO 8601 with offset, RFC 2822 and relative time.
Timestamp to date and date to timestamp.
Convert tens of thousands of timestamps in one go.
Flags the year 2038 limit, impossible times and wrong units.

example.title: Worked example: New Year in different zones
example.text: Type 1767225600. The tool detects seconds and shows ISO 8601 (UTC) 2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z. In New York it is still Wednesday 31 December 2025 at 7:00 PM, and choosing Asia/Kolkata shows 2026-01-01T05:30:00.000+05:30. Going the other way, picking 1 January 2026 00:00 with time zone UTC gives back 1767225600.

tips: If a date comes out in 1970 or far in the future, the unit is probably wrong; choose it under Unit.
JavaScript Date.now() gives milliseconds; most Unix tools and databases use seconds.
Store and send times in UTC and convert to local time only when showing them to people.
ISO 8601 with an offset, like 2026-01-01T05:30:00+05:30, is the safest text format to share times between systems.
Use the batch box to convert a column copied from a spreadsheet.
problems: You probably pasted milliseconds or a small number as seconds, or a value of 0. Check the Unit.
It says the timestamp is out of range
Dates can only be about 270,000 years from 1970. The number is likely in nanoseconds or microseconds; choose that unit.
The local time is an hour off
Check that the right time zone is chosen, and remember daylight saving time differs by date and country.
The time I picked does not exist
On the day clocks go forward, an hour is skipped in that zone. Pick a time outside the gap.
